![load](results/fig_load.png)

**3d. Answer quality and tokens per answer, on real Groq.** There are 20 easy questions (`data/questions.json`) and 9 hard ones (`data/questions_hard.json`) that I wrote to hit the traps in these papers. Altogether 23 are answerable and 6 are not. The rubric is frozen in `data/RUBRIC.md`: a question scores 1 if the facts are correct and it cites the gold paper and page (±1 page), and 0.5 if the facts are right but the citation is wrong or missing. An unanswerable question scores 1 only if the answer says "the papers don't say" without making a forbidden claim. Tokens per answer counts every model call for that question (classify, draft, and any loop or verify), taken from the API's `usage` field.

One thing to be upfront about: the first run scored 100% on the easy set, so it couldn't tell settings apart. I wrote the hard set after seeing that, and froze it before running any other setting. Then the 120B's daily tokens ran out during the first hard-set comparison. Those four runs are kept as `eval_tpdexhausted_*`, and every hard-set setting was rerun with the 20B drafting (those rows are marked 20B).

{{snip_quality}}

Across all 9 evaluation runs there were no confidently wrong answers and no declines. Every failure was a safe one: abstaining when the evidence was weak or badly extracted, or leaving out a citation. With 9 questions per hard-set row, one question is 11 points, so differences of one or two questions are noise. The same setting scored 72.2% on the 120B and 83.3% on the 20B.

**Things I wouldn't have guessed without running it:**
1. Groq has a 200,000 tokens-a-day limit on `gpt-oss-120b` that shows up in no response header, only in a 429 body. At about 2.3k tokens an answer that caps the 120B at roughly 85 answers a day, whatever the 1,000 requests a day in the headers suggests.
2. The 30 requests-a-minute limit is also missing from every header.
3. The "small, fast" model was slower. The 20B's median time to first token was 706.9 ms against 420.9 ms for the 120B, and p95 was 1,678.3 against 736.6 ms.
4. Groq's own `queue_time` (53.3 to 941.8 ms in my real logs) was often larger than its compute time (70.8 to 247.8 ms).
5. A burst of 20 requests at free-tier capacity gets only 3 full answers, because the token bucket holds 7,200 tokens, which is about 3 answers.

**The overload policy, before and after the load test showed it was flawed.** My first version estimated the wait without counting requests already in the queue. In a burst everyone queued up until their deadline and only then got the fallback. On top of that, the server's deadline equalled the user's patience, so some users left just before their answer arrived. Those runs (patience and deadline both 25 s) are kept in `logs/run1_before_queue_aware/`:

{{snip_before_fix}}

After I made the estimate count the queue and gave the server a deadline 3 s inside the user's patience (compare the 3b and 3c rows above), the median first-token time in the free-tier burst dropped from 20,799.6 ms to 26.2 ms. In the 10× overload run, users giving up went from 15 to 0. This isn't a controlled A/B: patience differed (25 s versus 20 s) and the timing differs between seeds. But the direction and size of the effect are clear.

**Did it meet "fast"?** Steady load: yes (at 10×, p50 1,324.5 ms and p95 4,465.3 ms). Sustained overload: yes, p95 was 6,877.6 ms, under the 8 s target. The 150-request burst at 10×: no. Latencies for the fallback replies are fine, but the full answers that were admitted had a p95 time to first token of 13,231.3 ms. The wait estimate is too optimistic for requests that get admitted just under the 40% threshold. I didn't tune it further.

## 4. Where the time goes

The slow request I traced is `real_steady2-0000` (real Groq, 20B). It took 5,217.5 ms to the first byte, the slowest of the 4 in that run. You can reproduce the breakdown with `python scripts/breakdown.py real_steady2`, which also prints the full event timeline. All timestamps come from `perf_counter` on one machine.

| part | ms | how I know |
|---|---:|---|
| before the server saw the request (client to ASGI) | 3,508.8 | client `arrive` versus server `enqueue`. The loop monitor logged stalls of 1,394 and 416 ms inside that window and three more (600, 1,170, 778 ms) in the 3 s before the request arrived. This was the first request of the run, so a cold connection too |
| waiting in my limiter queue | 12.3 | what's left after the other rows; the limiter had capacity (no 429, no queue) |
| provider calls | 1,683.3 | `send` to `last_token`: classify 1,028.6 plus draft 653.8 |
| of which Groq-reported compute / Groq-side queue | 322.0 / 432.4 | API `usage.total_time` 146.4 + 175.6; `usage.queue_time` 378.6 + 53.8 |
| local retrieval | 13.0 | `step_start` and `step_end` for retrieve |
| retrying (backoff) | 0.0 | no `retry` events |

All of the delay came before the first token. The answer is held until the deterministic check passes, so nothing reached the user before `user_first_token` at 5,215.8 ms. The last provider token arrived at 5,215.5 ms, and writing out the reply took about 0.1 ms more. The provider's own first-token events (classify at 1,026.2 ms, draft at 649.6 ms) are earlier and sit inside the provider-calls row. So nearly all of this request's slowness was on my side of the network: a cold first request on a stalled laptop, not the Groq tail.

An earlier real run (`real_steady`, slowest request 9,018.8 ms) had a BM25 search that took 937 ms when it normally takes about 3 ms, which is the same signature. That is why I added the provider-timing and loop-lag instrumentation, and I could only pin the cause down properly in the second run.

## 5. When a limit is hit

**Per-minute limits.** Tokens (8,000 a minute) are the one that binds. Requests (30 a minute) almost never do. The limiter keeps its own token buckets, sized from response headers and from 429 bodies. It learns the RPM limit from a 429 body, since no header has it. When a request arrives, it estimates the wait including everyone ahead of it:
- under 15% of the user's remaining time: normal path;
- under 40%: degraded, meaning the classify call is skipped, top-k goes from 5 to 3, and the loop and LLM verify are skipped. The answer is *delayed* but still comes from the model;
- 40% or more: no model call. If retrieval coverage is at least 0.6, the user gets a *weaker answer* immediately (quoted passages). Otherwise the request is *dropped*, with an honest "I'm at capacity and couldn't find a passage that clearly answers this".

Requests already admitted are never dropped because of load. Continuations run at priority 0 because their tokens are already spent, so an answer that has started will finish.

Who gets what depends on arrival order. Counts per quarter of the burst, earliest first (`results/tables.md`, section C):
- Free-tier burst of 20: the first quarter got 3 full answers and 2 fallbacks, and every later quarter got 5 fallbacks.
- 10× burst of 150: quarter 1 got 29 full answers, 8 fallbacks and 1 gave up; quarter 2 got 9 full and 28 fallbacks; quarters 3 and 4 got 36 fallbacks each (plus 1 and 2 shed).

I chose first-come-first-served among what the budget can pay for, because the alternative (letting everyone queue) made everyone wait and some leave (see the before/after in section 3).

**Per-day limit.** The daily limit that actually binds is tokens (200k), not requests (1,000). The limiter treats both as a daily wall. Once the wall is hit, whether I told it in config or it learned it from the first 429 body, no new model call starts. New arrivals get the quoted-passages reply if retrieval clearly matched, or an honest decline if not. Requests already past classification may still finish. A TPD 429 is never retried inside the deadline (its `retry-after` was 648 s). In the stand-in with a 40,000-token budget (`s_daily_known` and `s_daily_learned`), 20 requests got full answers and then 34 got fallbacks at about 20 to 30 ms median. Learning the limit from the 429 instead of being told cost exactly one request that ran into the wall.

{{snip_compact_daily}}

## 6. Retrieval: quality versus cost

I tried BM25, dense retrieval (`bge-small-en-v1.5`, with cached embeddings) and dense plus a cross-encoder rerank (`ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`, pool of 20). I crossed these with chunk size and top-k: 1,200 characters with 5 chunks, 600 with 8, 2,400 with 3, and a degraded 1,200 with 3. There were two measurements. The first is retrieval only: does a chunk from the gold paper and gold page (±1) appear among the retrieved chunks, over the 23 answerable questions, with no model calls. The second is answer quality with the real model (table 3d above).

{{snip_retrieval}}

- **I chose A: BM25, 1,200-character chunks, 200 overlap, top-k 5.** It finds the gold page 95.7% of the time at a median search time of 2.5 ms. The reranker reaches 100%, but its median search takes 8,254.6 ms (on CPU, in an executor, and cross-paper questions search twice). That is several times the length of the whole model call and would break the latency target on its own.
- Dense retrieval was slower (195.8 ms) and worse, both at finding the gold page (91.3%) and on end-to-end quality: 80.0% versus 100% on the easy set, and 66.7% versus 83.3% on the hard set. Its misses were false abstentions, which is the safe way to fail.
- Smaller chunks (D) lost context and scored 61.1% on the hard set. Bigger chunks with k=3 (E) hurt retrieval (82.6%), because three 2,400-character chunks were often the wrong three.
- I don't report user-visible time to first token per setting. The evaluation used a 300 s deadline so questions would queue behind the token limit, which makes each one take about 21 s. That is a pacing artefact and not a latency. What I can report is the provider's draft time to first token, p50 685.0 to 1,252.6 ms across rows in table 3d, and the local search latency in the table above.
- **Near a limit,** top-k drops from 5 to 3 (setting F: gold page found 91.3% instead of 95.7%, context 3,567 characters instead of 5,902, roughly 40% fewer prompt tokens, search 1.7 ms). The query-rewrite loop and classify call are skipped. If no model call is allowed at all, the answer is built from the highest-overlap sentences of the top 3 chunks.

## 7. Where this library fools a naive retriever

1. **Tables and numbers come out of the PDF scrambled.** "How many parameters does the big Transformer model have?" has the answer (213M) only in the last row of Table 3. It was answered correctly in 1 of 6 runs. The others abstained or got it wrong, and the abstentions are the safe failure. "How many layers and what model dimension does Moshi's Depth Transformer use?" (6 layers, 1,024) lives in a table whose cell labels are separated from their values. Gold-page retrieval missed it in every setting except the reranker, and answers were half right (0.5) when the model did find it. Only the 2,400-character setting, which keeps a whole table row together with its header, got the first question.
2. **The same words show up in all three papers.** "Transformer", "attention", "heads" and "layers" appear everywhere (Moshi has a Temporal and a Depth Transformer; H-Net compares against Transformer baselines). For "How many attention heads does the base Transformer use?", BM25's top hits were the appendix "Attention Visualizations" (score 15.64) and the ablation table. The architecture page with `h = 8` (p.5) wasn't in its top 3, though dense retrieval ranked it first. My keyword-based paper filter and top-k 5 fix this case, but a plain top-3 would answer from the wrong place.
3. **Structure heuristics lie, and my own filter removed real text.** My heading detector labelled 11 chunks of the H-Net paper "2.95 Perplexity on HG38", which is a table row. It also labelled pages 24 to 31 "References", so the filter that drops references removed 26 of the 146 H-Net chunks, including the start of Appendix A (Related Work, p.31). A question like "What does Appendix A of the dynamic chunking paper say about related work?" would have part of its evidence deleted from the index. I didn't test that exact question, but you can check the exclusion in `data/chunks_1200_200.json`. Page numbers are the dependable citation anchor (the PDF page index matches the printed numbers in these three papers). Section names are not.

Two other questions sound answerable from memory but aren't: "How many TPUs were used to train the Transformer base model?" (the word never appears in any of the three papers; the paper says 8 P100 GPUs) and "English-to-Czech BLEU". They test the abstain path, and the clean runs handled them correctly.

## 8. Retries

**The policy** is in `relay/llm.py`:
- at most 3 attempts, with exponential backoff (base 0.5 s, cap 8 s) and full jitter, never shorter than a `retry-after` the server sent;
- no retry if the wait wouldn't fit in the request's remaining deadline;
- no retry of a daily-limit 429, which switches to the daily path instead. Only per-minute 429s, 5xx and timeouts are retried;
- a retry budget, so retries stay at or below 20% of first attempts over a rolling 30 s window and an incident can't multiply the load;
- a per-call timeout of min(12 s, remaining deadline), so a call that sends headers and then stalls gets cut and retried or replaced by the fallback;
- a failed verification triggers one regeneration, counted separately.

**A case where retrying made things worse.** In the stand-in with 30% injected failures, load at 110% of capacity and 113 identical arrivals per run (`s_retrysat_*`):

{{snip_compact_retry}}

{{snip_retry_calls}}

Unbounded retries (3 attempts, no budget) sent 277 provider calls for 113 users, against 228 with no retries, and reserved 411,873 tokens against 285,255 (44.4% more). In return they completed 4 more full answers (81 versus 77), while p95 time to first token more than doubled (8,530.1 ms versus 4,037.5 ms; p50 2,022.1 versus 1,138.4 ms). The 20% budget cost less but at this load still didn't help: 75 full answers, 2 fewer than no retries, with p95 at 6,269.2 ms.

At 80% load (the rows above, 0.4 req/s) the picture is different. Retries raised full answers from 55 to 64 to 72 out of 82 but tripled median time to first token (817.8 to 2,459.1 ms). That is a genuine tradeoff and not a loss. One caveat: the stand-in charges tokens on injected failures. If the real service doesn't, the token cost is overstated (the latency effect isn't). No retries happened in the real runs (about 470 requests, no 5xx). The one real retry decision I saw was declining to retry a 648-second TPD `retry-after`.

## 9. What the person sees

At 3 pm the daily budget is gone. A waiting person gets this reply in about 20 to 30 ms (median 22.8 to 28.4 ms over all requests in the two stand-in daily runs, and 16.2 to 19.2 ms for the fallback replies alone). It's the actual text from the daily-budget run, taken from the `answer` field of a `done` event with status `extractive_daily`:

> *Our language-model budget for today is used up, so I can't write a summary right now. Here are the most relevant passages from the papers, quoted verbatim:*
> *"On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature." [C:attention:1]*
> *"6 Results 6.1 Machine Translation On the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, the big transformer model (Transformer (big) in Table 2) outperforms the best previously reported models (including ensembles) by more than 2.0 BLEU, establishing a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.4." [C:attention:22]* (a third passage follows)

If retrieval didn't clearly match the question, they get this instead: *"Today's model budget is used up and I couldn't find a passage that clearly answers this. Please try again tomorrow."* Requests that were already past their first model call when the budget ran out are allowed to finish normally.

Two weaknesses I know about. The quoted passages are only as relevant as BM25's coverage score lets them be; in `s_daily_learned` one reply quoted a figure caption. And the message says "tomorrow" when the real limit is a rolling window (a 1,962-token request was told to wait 648 s), so "try again in a few minutes" would be more accurate. I left both as they are.

## 10. What I'm unsure about, what I left out, what I learned

**My least certain assumption** is that the stand-in's behaviour under high concurrency, and its injected failures, represent the real service. The slowdown is a straight line through two measured points (4-way and 8-way), and the failure and stall rates are guesses, since I saw no real failure in about 470 requests. If that's wrong, the 10× latency tails and every retry-cost number in section 8 would move. The policy conclusions (count the queue when shedding, never retry a daily 429) don't depend on it, but the size of the "retries made it worse" effect does. A close second is the assumption that Groq charges `prompt + max_tokens` up front. If it charges actual usage instead, my limiter leaves roughly a quarter of the quota unused.

**Two things I chose not to build:**
1. *The Gemini fallback.* It's configured (`providers.gemini`) but I never ran or measured it. Groq stayed usable once I changed models, and a second provider would bring a second set of unknown limits to be unsure about.
2. *Request hedging for slow calls* (sending a duplicate after the p95 time and taking whichever answers first). On a clean service it would help the tail, but on a quota this tight it burns tokens, which is the same failure section 8 shows for unbounded retries. I also didn't build a persistent or multi-process limiter, since the service is single-node by design.

**Something new I learned:** TODO(Vaatsalya): write this yourself, in your own words. +2. **Retrieve.** BM25 over 1,200-character chunks with 200 characters of overlap, each carrying its page and section. A keyword check picks which paper to search. The search runs in an executor so it can't block the event loop.

+3. **Decide.** This is the branch. If few of the query's terms appear in the results (coverage under 0.6), it loops once: the small model rewrites the query and retrieval runs again. +5. **Verify.** A cheap deterministic check always runs: there is at least one citation, every cited id was actually retrieved, and every number in the answer appears in a cited chunk. +**What "fast" means here.** For a full model answer I set the target at a median time to first token of 2,500 ms or less and a p95 of 8,000 ms or less. -**The one decision that shaped it most: under pressure the system does *less optional work or answers from local text*; it never produces a cheaper, shakier generated answer.** Concretely the overload path is: (a) estimate the wait a *new* arrival will actually see, **including everyone already queued**; (b) if that wait would use more than 40% of the user's deadline, skip every model call and answer immediately from local retrieval, quoting the best sentences verbatim with citations, or, if retrieval did not clearly match (coverage < 0.6), say honestly that it can't answer right now; (c) requests already in flight outrank new ones (priority 0) because their tokens are already spent. +**The decision that shaped the most.** Under pressure the system does less work, or answers from local text. It never swaps in a cheaper, sloppier generated answer. -Other tradeoffs, stated where I made them:

-- *Fast vs good:* the deterministic check is always on (microseconds); the LLM check only when coverage is low (saves ~1 call per answer). -- *Good vs cheap:* top-k 5 normally, 3 when pressured; loop capped at 1 iteration (an unanswerable question otherwise burns calls confirming absence).
-- *Simple vs many-step:* step cap = 1 loop + 1 regeneration + 1 tool call per request.

-- *Cheap vs nobody turned away:* queue first (bounded by the deadline), then local-text fallback, then shed. Shed is rare by design: a fallback with citations is strictly more useful than "come back later" and costs no tokens.

+- *Fast versus good.* The deterministic check is always on because it costs microseconds. The LLM check only runs on low coverage, which saves about one call per answer. The small model handles classify, rewrite and verify, and the large one writes the draft. The small model turned out not to be faster on Groq (section 2), so its real value is that it draws on a separate quota pool.
+- *Good versus cheap.* Top-k is 5 normally and 3 under pressure. The loop is capped at one iteration, because otherwise an unanswerable question burns calls confirming that it's unanswerable.
+- *Simple versus many steps.* One loop, one regeneration and one tool call per request, at most.

+- *Cheap versus turning nobody away.* Queue first (within the deadline), then the local-text fallback, then shed. Shedding is rare by design, because a cited fallback is more useful than "come back later" and costs no tokens.

name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, master]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: requirements.txt
      # sentence-transformers (and torch) are only imported lazily for the dense
      # retrieval settings, which the tests don't touch, so skip the ~2 GB install.
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: grep -v '^sentence-transformers' requirements.txt > ci-requirements.txt && pip install -r ci-requirements.txt
      - name: Unit tests (limiter, citation checker, 429 parsing)
        run: pytest -q

  tables-match-logs:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: requirements.txt
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: grep -v '^sentence-transformers' requirements.txt > ci-requirements.txt && pip install -r ci-requirements.txt
      - name: Regenerate tables and README from logs
        run: |
          python scripts/make_tables.py
          python scripts/build_readme.py
      - name: Fail if committed tables or README differ from the logs
        run: git diff --exit-code -- results/tables.md README.md

  no-secrets:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Look for API keys in tracked files
        run: |
          if git grep -nE 'gsk_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}|AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{30,}' -- . ':!.github'; then
            echo "A key-shaped string is committed. Remove it and rotate the key."; exit 1
          fi
          if git ls-files --error-unmatch .env 2>/dev/null; then
            echo ".env is tracked."; exit 1
          fi

I added `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and updated `.gitignore`. I haven't run the workflow on GitHub, and I didn't run it locally either. I did check locally that the table scripts import nothing heavy and that `scripts/make_tables.py` followed by `scripts/build_readme.py` gives byte-identical output. I also left your own `.gitignore` change in place. It no longer ignores `papers/*.pdf`, so the PDFs will be committed.

The workflow has three jobs. It runs on pushes to `main` or `master`, and on pull requests.
- **tests:** Installs the dependencies and runs `pytest`. It leaves out `sentence-transformers`, because that pulls in torch and about 2 GB, and it is imported lazily only for the dense-retrieval settings, which the tests never touch.
- **tables-match-logs:** Re-runs `scripts/make_tables.py` and `scripts/build_readme.py`, then fails if `results/tables.md` or `README.md` differ from what is committed. This enforces the brief's rule that every table can be recomputed from the logs.
- **no-secrets:** Fails if a key-shaped string (`gsk_…` or `AIza…`) or a tracked `.env` turns up. This is a backstop, and `.gitignore` is the main protection.

The `tables-match-logs` job means that if you edit `README.md` directly instead of `README.template.md`, CI will fail. That includes filling in your TODO sections, so put those in the template and run `python scripts/build_readme.py`. Also, if you re-run any experiment, re-run both scripts and commit the results.

I also added to `.gitignore`:
- `ci-requirements.txt` (the temp file CI writes),
- coverage output,
- `act/`,
- `*.log.tmp`.

Alright everything done , now from the very scratch of everything , explain to me what was required to be done and what did you do and why  ? , what exactly it resulted it , what the results meant ? ,what different things you tried and what were the results ?, phase by phase , lets start with phase 1 first , also please DO NOT use complicted terminologies , use PLAIN english and be brief

There were roughly six phases. I'll go through them one at a time, starting with phase 1.

1. Understand the task and measure the real Groq service.
2. Build a fake Groq (the "stand-in") that behaves like the real one.
3. Build the question-answering pipeline.
4. Stress test it with heavy traffic.
5. Check answer quality and compare ways of searching the papers.
6. Write it all up.

## Phase 1: what we had to do, and what I found

**The task, in plain words.** Build a service that answers questions about three research papers and cites where each answer came from. It has to keep working when the AI provider (Groq) is slow, fails, or tells us "too many requests". You then test it under heavy traffic and report honestly what happened.

**The problem with testing.** The free Groq plan has small limits. If I hammered the real service, I'd use up the quota. So the plan was to measure the real service carefully once, then build a fake copy of it and do the heavy testing there.

**What I did, and why:**
1. **Picked the models.** I first assumed two Llama models, but Groq returned "not found" (404). I asked Groq what it actually offers and switched to `gpt-oss-20b` (small) and `gpt-oss-120b` (large). I wanted a small model for cheap jobs and a large one for writing answers.
2. **Downloaded the three papers** and saved their fingerprints (hashes), so anyone can check they have the same files.
3. **Measured the real speed**, with 15 short requests per model.
4. **Found the limits** by deliberately sending 40 requests in a burst. I kept it to 40 so I wouldn't waste quota.

**What came out:**

| Finding | Number |
|---|---|
| Requests per minute | 30 |
| Tokens per minute (tokens are the AI's unit of text) | 8,000 |
| Requests per day | 1,000 |
| Tokens per day | 200,000 (found later, by accident) |
| 40-request burst | 30 worked, 10 were rejected and told to retry in 2 seconds |
| Speed | 20B model: 707 ms to start answering; 120B model: 421 ms |

**What it means:**
- **The real bottleneck is tokens, not requests.** One answer uses about 2,000 to 2,300 tokens. That's only about 3 answers a minute and about 85 a day. The "1,000 requests a day" figure is misleading.
- **Some limits are hidden.** The 30-a-minute and 200k-a-day limits don't appear in the response headers (the extra information that comes with every reply). You only see them inside an error message, after you hit them.
- **The "small, fast" model was slower.** I'd assumed smaller meant faster. It didn't, so its main value is that it has a separate quota.

Everything in later phases is built on these numbers.

Ready for phase 2 (the fake Groq) when you are.
ready

## Phase 2: the fake Groq (the "stand-in")

**What was needed.** The brief wanted a copy of Groq that I control, so I can test heavy traffic without using the real quota. It had to be slow sometimes, fail sometimes, say "too many requests" with a wait time, slow down when busy, stream answers word by word, and run out of daily budget.

**What I did, and why:**
1. **Built a small web server (`standin/server.py`) that looks exactly like Groq.** The pipeline only needs a different web address to talk to it instead of the real one. That means the same code gets tested, with no special test mode.
2. **Copied the real numbers from phase 1.** The start-up delay and the typing speed are drawn from the real measurements. The limits are the same: 30 requests a minute, 8,000 tokens a minute, 1,000 a day and 200k a day. Each model has its own separate allowance, as on the real service.
3. **Copied how Groq says no.** When you go over a limit, it replies "429" with a wait time. It puts the kind of limit only in the message text, as the real one does.
4. **Added trouble on purpose:**
   - **Slow-but-successful calls:** some replies take 8 times longer.
   - **Stalls:** it says "OK", then goes silent.
   - **Errors:** some 500 errors.
   - **Busy slowdown:** the more requests at once, the slower each one gets.
5. **Made every run record its own settings**, so you can see exactly what each test was run against.

**What came out.** The fake behaves like the real one on the things I measured. It copies the speed pattern, the limits, and the error messages.

**What it means, and where it's weak.** I couldn't measure everything on the real service, so some parts are my guesses:
- **Failures and stalls are made up.** In about 470 real requests I saw zero errors and zero stalls, so how often I make the fake fail is invented.
- **The busy slowdown is a straight line drawn from only two tests** (4 and 8 requests at once). At very high load it's a rough shape and not a prediction.
- **The real Groq has its own waiting line inside it,** and the fake doesn't.
- **The token counting is a guess.** I think Groq counts the maximum possible answer length up front, not what's actually used.
- **It ignores answer quality.** It returns canned text.

So later results from the fake are good for comparing choices, such as which policy copes better. They aren't exact predictions of what Groq would do.

Ready for phase 3 (the question-answering pipeline)?
ready

## Phase 3: the question-answering pipeline

**What was needed.** A service that takes a question and returns a cited answer. It needed at least 4 steps, one tool call, one "decide" step or loop, and a search step. It also had to be able to say "the papers don't say".

**What I built, in order:**
1. **Understand the question.** The small model works out what's being asked and what to search for.
2. **Search the papers.** The papers are split into small pieces (chunks), each with its page number. A keyword search finds the best five.
3. **Decide.** If the search results match the question poorly, it rewrites the question and searches once more (that's the loop). If the question points at a specific section, it calls a small tool to fetch that section. I made that tool fail or run slow a few times on purpose, so the failure handling really gets used.
4. **Write the answer.** The large model writes it and must cite sources like `[C:paper:3]`. If the evidence isn't there, it must say "the papers don't say".
5. **Check it.** Before anyone sees the answer, a quick check runs: it has a citation, the cited pieces really were retrieved, and every number in the answer appears in those pieces. If the check fails, the model gets one retry. If that fails too, it declines honestly.
6. **Deliver it.**

**The rate limiter I wrote by hand.** It tracks requests and tokens like a budget, and it learns the hidden limits from error messages. Requests already started get priority, so an answer that's begun is allowed to finish.

**The main design choice.** When things get busy, the system does less, or answers straight from the paper text. It never writes a sloppier answer with a weaker model. If the wait would be too long, it skips the model and quotes the best sentences from the papers, with citations. If even that doesn't match the question, it says honestly that it can't answer right now.

**Retries.** There are at most 3 tries, with a growing pause between them. It never retries past the user's deadline. It never retries a daily-limit error, since that would wait about 11 minutes. Retries are capped at about 20% of calls, so a bad moment can't snowball.

**What it means.** Correctness is the floor, and speed and completeness are what give way. A user may get a plainer answer, but never a wrong one that looks confident.

**Bugs found while building it:**
- **Citation brackets:** my citation reader only understood plain brackets `[ ]`. The model sometimes used fancy brackets `【 】`, so 12 of 20 questions got wrongly declined. I fixed it and kept the bad run in the logs.
- **Hidden daily limit:** the 120B model's daily tokens ran out, which ruined four test runs. I made each model track its own limit, taught the limiter to learn limits from error messages, and reran those tests on the 20B.

Ready for phase 4 (the stress tests)?
ready

## Phase 4: the stress tests

**What was needed.** Prove how the service behaves under heavy traffic. That meant a separate tool that sends requests, at least 3 traffic patterns, and raw logs of everything.

**What I did:**
1. **Built a separate load generator.** It sends requests on its own schedule and doesn't wait for earlier ones to finish. That matters, because real users don't wait politely. If it waited, a slow service would quietly get less traffic and look better than it is. Each simulated user also gives up after 20 seconds, like a real person would.
2. **Used three traffic patterns:**
   - **Steady:** a normal trickle, below capacity.
   - **Burst:** a big batch at once, then quiet.
   - **Overload:** constant traffic at several times capacity.
3. **Ran each at two sizes.** One used the real free-tier limits. The other used 10 times those limits, because at free-tier size even "steady" is only a few requests a minute.
4. **Kept real runs tiny** (4, 4 and 8 requests), to protect the quota. The heavy runs were on the fake Groq.

**Results:**
- **Steady load:** fine. At 10× limits, half of requests started answering within 1.3 s and 95% within 4.5 s.
- **Overload:** also fine. 95% started within 6.9 s, under my 8 s target.
- **Burst of 150 at 10×:** missed the target. Full answers had a slowest-5% wait of 13.2 s. The fallback replies were fast.
- **Free-tier burst of 20:** only 3 people got full answers. The rest got quoted-passage fallbacks. That is simply what the token budget pays for.
- **Daily budget used up:** the first 20 got full answers, then 34 got instant fallbacks in about 20 to 30 ms.

**The big discovery: my first design was wrong.** It estimated the wait without counting the people already in line. So in a burst, everyone queued up, waited close to their whole deadline, and only then got the weak fallback. Some users left just before their answer arrived.

I fixed it in two ways. The wait estimate now counts the line. The server also gives up 3 seconds before the user would. The result: in the free-tier burst, the typical wait for a first response fell from 20.8 s to 0.03 s. In the 10× overload run, the number of people giving up went from 15 to 0. I kept the old runs in the logs. It isn't a perfectly controlled comparison, but the improvement is clear.

**Retries can make things worse.** On a service that fails 30% of the time and is nearly full, unlimited retries sent 277 calls for 113 users (228 without retries) and used 44% more tokens. They gained only 4 more full answers, and the slowest-5% wait more than doubled. Capping retries at 20% did better on cost, but at that load it still didn't help. At lighter load, retries did help: full answers went from 55 to 72 out of 82, at the price of slower typical waits.

**Caveat.** Real-Groq runs were too small to prove much. Real runs also showed my laptop freezing for up to 1.4 s, which inflated some times. I added a monitor to catch that, so I could blame the laptop and not Groq.

## Phase 5: answer quality and comparing search methods

**What was needed.** Speed means nothing if the answers are wrong. The brief wanted at least 15 questions I wrote myself, a scoring rule fixed before comparing anything, and a fair comparison of different settings.

**What I did:**
1. **Wrote 20 easy questions,** including some the papers can't answer. These test whether the system honestly says "the papers don't say".
2. **Fixed the scoring rule up front** (`data/RUBRIC.md`):
   - 1 point: right facts and the right paper and page cited.
   - Half a point: right facts, wrong or missing citation.
   - Unanswerable questions: full marks only for saying "the papers don't say" without inventing anything.
3. **Ran it on the real Groq.** The first run scored 100%.
4. **Wrote 9 harder questions,** because 100% can't tell settings apart. I wrote them after seeing that result, and I froze them before running any other setting. This is stated openly in the write-up. The hard questions target the traps in these papers: numbers in tables, words repeated across papers, and so on.

**Search methods compared:**
- **A: Keyword search (BM25), normal-sized pieces.** This is the one I chose.
- **B: Meaning-based search (dense).**
- **C: Meaning-based search plus a second reranking pass.**
- **D: Smaller pieces.**
- **E: Bigger pieces, only 3 returned.**
- **F: Keyword search with only 3 pieces, the fewer-results mode used under pressure.**

**Results:**

| Method | Found the right page | Speed per search | Hard-set score (20B model) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A: keyword | 95.7% | 2.5 ms | 83.3% |
| B: meaning-based | 91.3% | 196 ms | 66.7% |
| C: with reranking | 100% | 8,255 ms | 77.8% |
| D: smaller pieces | – | – | 61.1% |
| E: bigger pieces, 3 returned | 82.6% | – | 66.7% |
| F: fewer results | 91.3% | 1.7 ms | – |

**What it means:**
- **Keyword search won.** The reranker is slightly more accurate but takes 8 seconds per search, which would break the speed target by itself. Meaning-based search was slower and worse here.
- **Zero confident wrong answers in every run.** All failures were safe ones, such as saying "the papers don't say" when the evidence was weak, or leaving out a citation.
- **Small differences are noise.** With only 9 hard questions, one question is 11 points. The same setting scored 72.2% on the big model and 83.3% on the small one.

**Where the papers fool a simple search:**
- **Tables:** numbers come out of the PDF scrambled. The question about the big model's size (213M) was answered correctly only 1 time in 6.
- **Repeated words:** "Transformer" and "attention" appear in all three papers, so a search can pull the wrong page.
- **My own mistake:** my reference-removal filter wrongly deleted 26 of 146 chunks of the third paper, including the start of Appendix A.

**Limits to remember.** The 120B's daily quota ran out partway, so all hard-set settings were rerun on the 20B. The invalid runs are kept and labelled.

Ready for phase 6 (the write-up)?
ready

## Phase 6: the write-up

**What was needed.** A report with 12 sections in a fixed order, where every table can be recomputed from the raw logs. Three sections had to be personal: what you learned, your feedback on Vaani, and how you worked with the assistant.

**What I did:**
1. **Kept every number traceable.** `make_tables.py` rebuilds every table from the raw logs, and `build_readme.py` fills them into the README. Nothing in the tables is typed by hand.
2. **Checked the prose against the tables.** I found and fixed several slips: a wrong sum, the answerable/unanswerable counts, a wrong number of requests, and an inexact quote.
3. **Kept the failures in.** The bad runs stay in `logs/` under names that say what went wrong: the citation-bracket bug, the exhausted daily tokens, and the laptop freeze. The write-up lists them.
4. **Wrote the 12 sections:**
   - What I built and why.
   - The real service versus the stand-in.
   - Results.
   - Where the time goes.
   - When a limit is hit.
   - Retrieval choices.
   - How the papers fool a simple search.
   - Retries.
   - What the person sees.
   - Uncertainties, what I left out, what I learned.
   - Vaani feedback.
   - How I worked with the assistant.
5. **Rewrote it in plain first-person prose** so it doesn't read machine-made.
6. **Added the repo hygiene:** a `.gitignore` (keeps `.env` and keys out), and a CI check on GitHub. CI runs the tests, confirms the tables still match the logs, and scans for leaked keys.

**What it means.** Anyone can rerun the scripts and get the same tables. The report also says plainly where the stand-in is a guess and where the real samples were too small.

**What is still yours.** I left five TODOs, because the brief wants your own words there:
- What you newly learned.
- Your feedback on Vaani, after you visit vaani.dev.
- Copying the conversation transcript into `docs/` yourself. I couldn't do it, because it was blocked as a sensitive source.
- Which three prompts mattered, one mistake you caught, and one decision you overruled.
- What's distinctly yours.

Put these in `README.template.md`, then run `python scripts/build_readme.py`. If you edit `README.md` directly, CI will fail.

That's all six phases. If you want, I can go over anything again in simpler words, or help you draft notes for your own sections.

alright so lets trace calls from the users in different scenario's 1.normal 2.burst 3.overload what is the overall workflow of our pipeline in these three circumstances in PLAIN english and in depth ( also explain me how the system handles failures in these different scenario's )

I'll follow one request through the system first, then show how each scenario changes the route.

## The basic journey of one question

1. **Arrival.** The user's question reaches the server. It starts a countdown: a deadline of 17 s. The simulated user gives up at 20 s, so the server stops 3 s before that.
2. **Check the line.** The system asks: "If I send this to the AI now, how long will it wait, counting everyone already waiting?" This is the key step, and everything else follows from it.
3. **Understand.** The small model works out what's being asked and what to search for.
4. **Search.** The system searches the paper text and takes the best 5 pieces. This takes a few milliseconds.
5. **Decide.** If the pieces match the question poorly, it rewrites the question and searches once more. If the question points at a section, it calls the "fetch section" tool.
6. **Write.** The big model writes an answer with citations.
7. **Check.** A quick check confirms there's a citation, the cited piece was really retrieved, and every number appears in it.
8. **Deliver.** Only now does the user see anything.

Every AI call goes through my rate limiter first. It keeps a budget of requests and tokens, and it makes calls wait if the budget is empty.

## Scenario 1: normal traffic

**What happens.** At step 2 the line is empty or short. The estimated wait is under 15% of the user's time, so the request takes the normal path. It makes about 2 or 3 AI calls (understand, write, and sometimes a second try), uses about 2,000 to 2,300 tokens, and gets a full answer.

**What the user sees.** A cited answer, or an honest "the papers don't say". With the 10× limits, half of requests got their first response in about 1.3 s, and 95% in under 4.5 s.

**Failures here:**
- **Brief 429 ("slow down"):** the limiter waits the time the server asked for, plus a random bit so everyone doesn't retry at once. It tries at most 3 times, and only if the wait fits inside the user's remaining time.
- **Server error or a stall:** a call that goes silent is cut off after 12 s, or sooner if the deadline is closer. Then it retries, or the system falls back to quoting the papers. I invented these failures in the stand-in, since the real service never failed in my tests.
- **A failed check:** the model gets one chance to rewrite. If it fails again, the user gets an honest "I couldn't verify an answer", not a guess.
- **The fetch-section tool breaks:** it times out after 3 s, and the system carries on without it using the normal search results.
- **Answer missing from the papers:** the model says so. That's a correct result, and it counts as a success.

## Scenario 2: burst

**What happens.** A big batch arrives within seconds, far more than the token budget can pay for. At step 2, the system counts the line each time:
- **First few arrivals:** wait is short, so they get full answers. In the free-tier burst of 20, that was only 3 people, because the budget holds about 3 answers' worth of tokens.
- **Middle arrivals** (wait under 40% of their time): they get a lighter version. It skips the understanding call, searches for 3 pieces instead of 5, and skips the extra checks. They wait longer but still get an AI-written answer.
- **Later arrivals** (wait 40% or more): the AI is skipped entirely. If the search clearly matches the question, they instantly get the best sentences quoted straight from the papers, with citations, in about 20 to 30 ms. If not, they get an honest "I'm at capacity and couldn't find a clear answer".

In the 10× burst of 150, the first quarter got 29 full answers, 8 fallbacks and 1 who gave up. The second quarter got 9 full answers and 28 fallbacks. The last two quarters got only fallbacks (plus 3 turned away).

**The rule underneath.** First come, first served, among what the budget can pay for. Anyone already in the middle of an answer goes first (priority 0), because their tokens are already spent. So started answers always finish.

**Why it works this way.** My first version didn't count the line, so everyone waited until their deadline and then got the weak answer, and some left just before it arrived. Counting the line fixed that. The typical wait dropped from 20.8 s to 0.03 s.

**Failures here:**
- **Many 429s at once:** the limiter spaces calls out, and retries stay within the 20% cap so they can't pile on.
- **Slow calls while busy:** the system won't retry past the deadline. It falls back to quoting.
- **Weak spot:** admitted full answers in the 150-burst still had a slowest-5% wait of 13.2 s, because the wait estimate was too optimistic for people admitted just under the 40% line. I didn't tune it further.

## Scenario 3: sustained overload

**What happens.** Traffic keeps coming at several times what the budget can handle, with no quiet gap to recover. The same decisions from scenario 2 repeat over and over. The line stays long, so most new arrivals fall into the "40% or more" bucket and get instant fallbacks. Only enough requests get through to use the budget. Because replies come back in milliseconds, nobody waits and then leaves. In the 10× overload run, 95% of first responses came in under 6.9 s and nobody gave up.

**The daily wall.** If the daily token budget runs out, the limiter learns it either from config or from the first error message that mentions it. After that no new AI call starts. New arrivals get the quote-the-papers reply, or an honest decline. Requests already past their first AI call may still finish. In the test, 20 people got full answers, then 34 got instant fallbacks. Learning the limit from the error cost exactly one request that hit the wall.

**Failures here:**
- **Daily-limit error:** never retried. The real "come back in" time was 648 s, far past any deadline.
- **Retry storms:** this is where retries hurt. At 30% failures and near-full load, unlimited retries sent 277 calls for 113 users and used 44% more tokens, for only 4 more full answers. The slowest-5% wait doubled. The 20% cap keeps this in check. At lighter load, retries did help.
- **Tokens wasted on failures:** the stand-in charges tokens on injected errors. I don't know whether Groq does, so the retry cost may be overstated.

## One-line comparison

| | Normal | Burst | Overload |
|---|---|---|---|
| Line | Empty | Long, then clears | Always long |
| Most users get | Full answer | A few full answers, then quoted fallbacks | Mostly quoted fallbacks |
| Wait | Seconds | Instant for fallbacks | Instant for fallbacks |
| Failure handling | Retry, cut off stalls, fall back | Space out calls, retry only within the cap | No retry of daily limit, strict cap, daily wall |
| Guarantee | Correct or honest | Same | Same |

Through all three, the guarantee is the same: a wrong answer is never presented as a confident one. What changes under pressure is how much work the user gets, not whether it's trustworthy.

All commands run from the project folder `C:\VSCode\VaaniAI`. The real key is read from `.env`, so you don't need to set anything. I checked the flags against the scripts but haven't run these exact commands just now.

**Start with the cheapest test.** It's one real question through the full pipeline, about 2,000 tokens.

1. Start the server pointed at real Groq (PowerShell):
   ```powershell
   .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
   $env:RELAY_PROVIDER = "groq"
   $env:RELAY_LOG = "logs/server_mytest.jsonl"
   uvicorn relay.server:app --port 8100
   ```
2. In a second terminal, ask a question:
   ```powershell
   curl.exe -N "http://127.0.0.1:8100/ask?q=How many attention heads does the base Transformer use?&req=t1"
   ```
   You should see a cited answer like `[C:attention:5]`. Try an unanswerable one too: `q=English-to-Czech BLEU`. You should get "the papers don't say".
3. Look at what really happened. Open `logs/server_mytest.jsonl`, which lists each step, each Groq call, the tokens used, and any retry or 429.

**Other tests, in order of quota cost:**
- **Quality on the real model** (about 20 questions, roughly 45k tokens):
  ```powershell
  python scripts/run_eval.py --provider groq --tag mytest_eval --large openai/gpt-oss-20b
  ```
  Use `--questions questions_hard` for the hard set. Pass `--large openai/gpt-oss-20b` so you don't spend the 120B's 200k daily tokens. The write-up's quality runs used the 20B as drafter.
- **A tiny real load test** (4 to 8 requests):
  ```powershell
  python scripts/run_load.py --provider groq --tag mytest_steady --shape steady --rate 0.03 --duration 120 --large openai/gpt-oss-20b
  python scripts/analyze.py mytest_steady
  ```
- **A burst on the real service,** 8 requests at once. It's fine to try but burns quota fast, and you will see 429s and fallbacks:
  ```powershell
  python scripts/run_load.py --provider groq --tag mytest_burst --shape burst --n 8 --window 3 --large openai/gpt-oss-20b
  ```
  Check the flags with `python scripts/run_load.py -h` first.
- **Probe the limits again** (about 40 requests, which deliberately triggers 429s): `python scripts/probe_groq.py --hit-limit`.

**Quota rules to keep in mind:**
- 8,000 tokens a minute means about 3 full answers a minute, so don't be surprised by waits.
- The 120B's daily 200k tokens may already be used today. Stay on the 20B.
- Don't run big load shapes on real Groq. Use the stand-in for those by leaving out `--provider groq`.

**If something looks wrong:**
- **Fallback quotes or "at capacity":** you're out of per-minute budget. Wait a minute.
- **"Budget for today is used up":** the daily wall. It resets gradually.
- **A request taking 5 s or more on its own:** check `loop_lag` events in the log. That's your laptop pausing, not Groq.

You pasted only the command with no output after it, so I'm guessing at the cause. Two things could be happening.

**1. It may be working, just slowly.** Nothing prints until the answer has been checked, which usually takes 1 to 5 seconds. If the cursor is still waiting, give it up to 10 seconds.

**2. The URL may be the problem.** Your question has spaces and a `?` inside the web address, and `curl` can mangle that and print nothing. Let curl encode it for you:

```powershell
curl.exe -N -G "http://127.0.0.1:8100/ask" --data-urlencode "q=How many attention heads does the base Transformer use?" --data-urlencode "req=t1"
```

If that still prints nothing, add `-i` to see the status code, for example `curl.exe -i -N -G ...`. A status of 422 means a parameter is missing or wrong. A status of 500 means the server hit an error.

If it still fails, run these two checks and paste what comes back:
- `curl.exe http://127.0.0.1:8100/health` should return a short OK message.
- Look at the terminal where uvicorn is running. Any error from your request would show there, and the last few lines of `logs/server_mytest.jsonl` will show whether the request arrived at all.

Also, use a new `req` value each time (`t2`, `t3`, …) so the log entries stay separate.

It worked. This was a real Groq call through the whole pipeline, and the answer is correct: the base Transformer uses 8 attention heads.

**What the output means**
- `status: answered, level: 0` means it took the normal path with no pressure. Level 0 is the full-quality route from the normal-traffic scenario.
- The text arrives word by word, but all at once, because the system holds it until the check passes. That's the verify-before-release behaviour.
- `[C:attention:12]` is a chunk id, not a page number. I checked: chunk 12 of the Attention paper is on **page 5**, in section 3.2.2. It contains the line "= 8 parallel attention layers, or heads". That is the correct source.
- `event: end` means the answer is finished.

**What happened behind the scenes** (from `logs/server_mytest.jsonl`)
1. **Classify:** the 20B model took about 0.8 s. It used 259 tokens.
2. **Retrieve:** about 10 ms. The decision was `draft`, with match confidence 1.0, so no rewrite loop was needed.
3. **Draft:** the 120B model took about 1.0 s. It used 1,904 tokens, and the limiter had reserved 2,314 for it up front.
4. **Check:** the deterministic check passed with no issues. The reply was released immediately.

The whole question took about 2 seconds and about 2,160 tokens, which fits the 2,000 to 2,300 estimate in the write-up. The 120B was used for the draft, so that call counts against its 200k daily tokens.

The last log line is a `loop_lag` of 112 ms. That's your laptop pausing briefly, not Groq.

**Things to try next**
- **Unanswerable:** `q=What is the English-to-Czech BLEU score?`. You should get "the papers don't say".
- **Table number:** `q=How many parameters does the big Transformer model have?`. This one is hard, so expect the system to abstain or get it wrong rather than answer confidently wrong. Use a new `req` each time.
- **Fallback path:** ask 4 or 5 questions quickly in a row. Once the per-minute token budget is empty, you should see `status: extractive…` and quoted passages instead of a model answer.
